narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 61.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the model judged failure more likely than success, which crossed the school’s risk threshold for admission. This is not a guarantee that you will fail, but it is the reason the application was rejected.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged near the sixth decile. That very low relative standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 35, slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37; in your case, however, this factor leaned toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90, below the accepted average of about 3.23, was the third most influential factor and also leaned toward passing. Even so, the third-year standing signal was stronger and outweighed those positive signals.

To strengthen a future application, ask admissions for feedback, focus on raising your academic standing through additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, and consult a pre-law advisor about whether retaking the LSAT is worthwhile. Consider applying more broadly to schools that review candidates holistically, and build a concrete bar-exam preparation plan so you can demonstrate readiness.
